# Preparation

We first load all packages and datasets and run the analysis and the manual check:

```{r}
#| output: false
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(pander)
source("02_analyse_licenses.R")

# 04 reads its own copy of the papers, so it runs in its own environment
manual_env <- new.env()
source("04_evaluate_manual_check.R", local = manual_env)
check <- manual_env$check

# numbers for the method text
readme_presence <- read.csv(file.path(MAT_DIR, "osf_readme_presence.csv"))
strata <- read.csv("data/manual_check_strata.csv")
pairs <- distinct(object_licenses, doi, osf_project)
n_shared_ids <- sum(table(pairs$osf_project) > 1)
crawl_dates <- range(object_licenses$checked)
n_components <- n_distinct(components$component_id[components$depth > 0])
n_github <- n_distinct(components$component_id[!is.na(components$github_repo)])

# pairs without a row in the deposit's documentation coding, by object type
doc_llm <- read.csv(file.path(MAT_DIR, "osf_documentation_llm.csv"))
doc_missing <- distinct(osf_files, doi, osf_project) |>
  anti_join(doc_llm, by = c("doi", "osf_project")) |>
  left_join(distinct(object_licenses, osf_project, holder_type), by = "osf_project")
```

# Method

## Population and objects

We build on Quintana's deposit (v1.1.0, <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22805418>) and use
his corpus, population and documentation coding unchanged. His corpus covers empirical
papers published in *Cognition*, the *Journal of
Experimental Social Psychology* (JESP), the *Journal of Memory and Language* (JML) and
*Psychological Science* in 2015, 2020 and 2025. We use the population of his
documentation analysis: the `r nrow(papers)` empirical papers that share materials on OSF
with a readable file listing (`osf_readme_presence.csv`).

The deposit's file listing (`osf_file_downloads.csv`) links `r n_distinct(pairs$doi)`
papers to `r n_distinct(pairs$osf_project)` distinct OSF objects (`r nrow(pairs)` paper and
object pairs; `r n_shared_ids` objects are linked by two papers). An object can be a
project, a component, a registration or a single file. Files carry no license, so a link to
a file is resolved to the project or registration that holds it, the same rule as in
Quintana's `collect_osf_documentation.R`. The papers of the population link
`r nrow(linked_objects)` of these objects.

## Data collection

We queried the OSF API (v2) for every linked object between `r crawl_dates[1]` and
`r crawl_dates[2]` (`01_collect_osf_licenses.R`). Licenses are therefore read at the crawl
date, not at publication. We considered five sources of a license:

1. **OSF license field.** Each project, component and registration has a license field,
   which OSF shows on the project page. We recorded the license of each linked object and
   walked all components below it, at any depth (`r n_components` components). We stored
   only whether a copyright holder is given, not the names.
2. **LICENSE files.** File names in the deposit's listing that contain `license` or
   `licence`, or that are `COPYING` or `COPYRIGHT` (alone or followed by a separator). The
   listing covers components at any depth and add-on storage, but for registrations only
   OSF storage.
3. **GitHub add-ons.** An OSF project can connect a GitHub repository as storage. For the
   `r n_github` nodes with such an add-on, we recorded the license GitHub detects in the
   repository. GitHub's `NOASSERTION`, a license file it cannot match, counts as a license.
4. **Descriptions.** The description of every linked object and of its direct components.
5. **READMEs.** The README files of the `r sum(readme_presence$has_readme)` papers whose
   file listing has one (names matching `readme`, `read me` or `read_me`, as in Quintana's
   `analyse_osf_readme.R`). The deposit lists file names without ids, so we walked each
   file tree again, including components, until all listed READMEs were found. PDF and
   Word files were converted to text.

Descriptions and READMEs were searched for `licen[sc]`. Each text with a match was coded by
hand (`r nrow(mentions)` texts, see [Coding schemes](#coding-schemes)). The passages are
other researchers' text, so we share only the coding and a link to each page.

## Definitions

A paper counts as **licensed** if at least one of its linked objects or their components
has a license in the OSF field, if there is a LICENSE file or a licensed GitHub add-on, or
if a description or README is coded as stating a license. On OSF, "No license" is an
explicit choice and counts as unlicensed; "Other" is a custom license and counts as
licensed. We also report the OSF license field on its own, as it is the only
machine-readable source and the one shown on the project page.

A paper can carry several **license types**, e.g. CC BY for data and MIT for code. We map
all of them to SPDX identifiers (<https://spdx.org/licenses>) and count each type once per
paper. The type of a LICENSE file is not read.

## Analysis

We report the share of licensed papers with exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% confidence
intervals, overall, per journal and per period (`02_analyse_licenses.R`). As licenses are
read at the crawl date, older papers had more time to gain a license, and differences
between years are hard to interpret. We therefore only compare papers from 2025 with
earlier papers: *Psychological Science* requires an open license for submissions from 2024.
2015 has few papers on OSF, so it is pooled with 2020. OSF also asks for a license when a
registration is created, which raises rates independently of journal policy, so we repeat
the comparison without registrations. Finally, we compare licensing between papers with and
without shared code (any code file in the deposit's listing) and between papers with and
without documentation as coded by Quintana (a README, or substantive reuse guidance in the
OSF description or wiki), the latter with Fisher's exact test.

## Manual check

To validate the crawl, `03_sample_manual_check.R` drew a stratified sample of
`r nrow(strata)` papers (`r round(100 * nrow(strata) / nrow(papers))`% of the population).
Each paper was assigned to one of five strata (@tbl-strata), in the order listed, so a paper
falls into the first stratum that applies. Cases where the crawl is most likely to err are
oversampled: the sample includes every paper in the first two strata and 15% of the papers
linking a registration or a single file. The rest of the sample is split over the last two
strata in proportion to their size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-strata
#| tbl-cap: "Strata of the manual check, in the order they are assigned, with the number of sampled papers."
stratum_info <- tibble(
  stratum = c("child, file or readme only", "no license chosen", "registration or file link",
              "licensed on OSF", "unlicensed"),
  definition = c("Licensed, but not in the OSF license field of a linked object",
                 "Unlicensed, with \"No license\" chosen on OSF",
                 "Links a registration or a single file",
                 "Licensed in the OSF license field of a linked object",
                 "All other papers")
)
stratum_info |>
  left_join(count(strata, stratum, name = "papers"), by = "stratum") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Stratum", "Definition", "Sampled papers"))
```

The coding sheet is in random order and does not show our coding or the stratum. Each
paper was coded by opening its OSF links and looking for a
license anywhere on the linked pages, including places the crawl does not cover (e.g. the
wiki). `04_evaluate_manual_check.R` compares this coding with the crawl: agreement and
Cohen's kappa for the OSF license field, and per stratum how often a license is stated
elsewhere.

## Coding schemes

### License mentions

Each row of `data/license_mentions.csv` is one description or README with at least one
match. Re-running `01` keeps the coding and leaves new texts empty; `02` warns if any are
uncoded and counts them as no license.

| Column | Coding |
|---|---|
| `states_license` | `yes` if the text states a license for the shared materials or for part of them (e.g. one tool); `no` for other uses of the word: licenses of third-party data or software (Matlab, LDC corpora), or "license" in another sense. |
| `license_name` | SPDX ids, several separated by `; ` (e.g. `CC-BY-4.0; GPL-3.0`). |
| `coding_note` | Reason for unclear cases. |

### Manual check

Each sampled paper was coded in `data/manual_check.csv` as follows.

| Column | Coding |
|---|---|
| `license_osf` | `yes` if a linked project or registration, or one of its direct components, shows a license on its OSF page; else `no`. "No license" counts as `no`. For a link to a single file, check the project or registration holding it. |
| `license_osf_name` | The license in the OSF license field, as SPDX id (e.g. `CC-BY-4.0`, `CC0-1.0`, `MIT`). Empty if `license_osf` is `no`. |
| `license_other` | `yes` if a license is stated anywhere else: a LICENSE or README file, the project description, the wiki, a deeper component, GitHub, or a page linked from the paper or project; else empty. |
| `license_other_where` | Where: `file`, `readme`, `description`, `wiki`, `component`, `github` (repository connected as storage) or `link` (repository or page only linked from the paper or the project). |
| `license_other_name` | The license stated there, as SPDX id (e.g. `MIT`); `unknown` if the type is unclear. |
| `checked_on` | Date of the check (licenses can change after the crawl). |
| `notes` | Anything unclear. |

# Results

## Licensing rates

Of the `r nrow(papers)` papers, `r sum(papers$licensed)`
(`r round(100 * mean(papers$licensed))`%) carry a license. @tbl-routes shows where these
licenses come from. Each licensed paper is counted once, under the first source in the
list that applies, so the sources add up to the licensed papers.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-routes
#| tbl-cap: "Source of the license, as number and percentage of all papers. Each paper is counted under the first source that applies."
route_n <- setNames(license_routes$n, license_routes$route)
tibble(
  source = c("OSF license field of a linked object",
             "OSF license field of a component",
             "LICENSE file",
             "GitHub add-on",
             "README",
             "Description",
             "**Licensed**",
             "**Not licensed**",
             "of which \"No license\" chosen on OSF",
             "**All papers**"),
  n = c(route_n[c("osf_object", "child_only", "license_file_only", "github_only",
                  "readme_only", "description_only")],
        sum(papers$licensed), sum(!papers$licensed), route_n[["no_license_chosen"]],
        nrow(papers))
) |>
  mutate(pct = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * n / nrow(papers))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Source", "Papers", "%"))
```

Without this order, `r route_n[["any_osf_field"]]` papers have a license in an OSF license
field (of an object or a component), `r route_n[["any_license_file"]]` a LICENSE file,
`r route_n[["any_github"]]` a licensed GitHub add-on, `r route_n[["any_readme"]]` a README
and `r route_n[["any_description"]]` a description that states a license.

@tbl-rates shows the share of licensed papers per journal and period, once for all linked
objects and once without registrations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rates
#| tbl-cap: "Licensed papers / all papers, with percentage and 95% CI."
rates_for_text |>
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%d/%d, %s", n_licensed, n, text),
         journal = if_else(journal == "all", "All journals", journal),
         period = if_else(period == "all", "All years", period)) |>
  select(objects, journal, period, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = objects, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Journal", "Period", "All objects", "Without registrations"))
```

@fig-main shows the share of licensed papers per journal before and after 2025 (a) and the
license types used (b). The SPDX identifiers are spelled out in @tbl-types.

```{r}
#| label: fig-main
#| fig-cap: "(a) Share of papers with OSF materials that include a license, per journal and for all journals together (dashed). (b) License types, each counted once per paper. Types used by fewer than five papers are pooled as Other. No license: papers without any license."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig
```

@fig-facets shows the same shares as panel (a) of @fig-main, one journal per panel and with
95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-facets
#| fig-cap: "Share of licensed papers per journal and period, with exact 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
fig_facets
```

@fig-dumbbell shows the change between the two periods as a dumbbell chart, with the number
of papers per journal and period in brackets. Panel (b) is the same as in @fig-main.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dumbbell
#| fig-cap: "(a) Share of licensed papers in 2015 and 2020 (open dot) and in 2025 (filled dot), with the number of papers in brackets. (b) License types, as in @fig-main."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig_dumbbell
```

## License types

@tbl-types lists all license types. Percentages refer to all `r sum(license_counts$n)` uses
of a license type, as a paper can carry more than one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-types
#| tbl-cap: "License types, each counted once per paper."
license_counts |>
  select(short, license_name, n, pct) |>
  kable(col.names = c("SPDX id", "Name on OSF", "Papers", "% of uses"))
```

## Code sharing and documentation

@tbl-doc compares licensing between papers with and without shared code, and between papers
with and without documentation. Documented papers are licensed more often (odds ratio
`r sprintf("%.1f", doc_test$estimate)`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.1f", doc_test$conf.int[1])`
to `r sprintf("%.1f", doc_test$conf.int[2])`, Fisher's exact test).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-doc
#| tbl-cap: "Licensed papers by code sharing and documentation, with 95% CI."
bind_rows(
  mutate(by_code, group = "Shares code", value = shares_code),
  mutate(by_doc, group = "Documented", value = documented)
) |>
  mutate(value = if_else(value, "yes", "no"),
         text = sprintf("%d%% [%d, %d]", pct, ci_low, ci_high)) |>
  select(group, value, n, n_licensed, text) |>
  kable(col.names = c("", "", "Papers", "Licensed", "% [95% CI]"))
```

## Manual check

@tbl-agreement compares the OSF license field in the manual check with the crawl. The two
agree for `r round(100 * mean(check$manual_osf == check$ours_osf))`% of the
`r nrow(check)` papers (Cohen's kappa
`r round(psych::cohen.kappa(cbind(check$manual_osf, check$ours_osf))$kappa, 2)`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-agreement
#| tbl-cap: "License in the OSF field, manual check (rows) against crawl (columns)."
agreement <- table(manual = check$manual_osf, crawl = check$ours_osf)
kable(as.data.frame.matrix(agreement), row.names = TRUE)
```

@tbl-strata-results shows per stratum how many papers are licensed by our coding and by the
manual check, and how many state a license only outside the OSF field.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-strata-results
#| tbl-cap: "Licensed papers per stratum, crawl and manual check."
check |>
  group_by(stratum) |>
  summarise(n = n(), licensed_ours = sum(licensed), licensed_manual = sum(manual_any),
            other_only = sum(manual_other & !manual_osf)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Stratum", "Papers", "Licensed (crawl)", "Licensed (manual)",
                      "Only outside the OSF field"))
```

# Limitations

- Licenses are read at the crawl date, not at publication; authors can add or change a
  license later.
- OSF asks for a license when a registration is created, and *Psychological Science*
  requires an open license for submissions from 2024. Both raise the 2025 rate without an
  author choosing a license, so rates are also reported with registrations left out.
- GitHub repositories linked in the paper or the OSF description, rather than connected as
  storage, are not checked. Many of them are third-party tools (e.g. PsychoPy) whose
  license says nothing about the shared materials.
- Papers linking private projects through view-only links are not covered: the keys are
  redacted in the deposit, and those papers are outside the population.
- READMEs and descriptions are only searched for "license" or "licence". A statement like
  "data: CC0" without that word is missed, as are licenses in the wiki, in files not named
  README, and in scanned PDFs. READMEs are read only for papers whose file listing in the
  deposit has one, and not all listed READMEs could be found for one registration.
  LICENSE files are found by name only. In the manual check, one paper stated a CC0 license
  inside a text file that links to the registration. We count such a paper as unlicensed,
  as reusers are unlikely to look for a license there.
- The comparisons with code sharing and documentation are descriptive. Licensed and
  documented papers may share causes, such as journal policy or the authors' general
  practices.

## A note on the deposit

`r nrow(doc_missing)` of the paper and object pairs in `osf_file_downloads.csv` have no row
in the deposit's `osf_documentation_llm.csv`
(`r sum(doc_missing$holder_type %in% "registrations")` of them registrations), from
`r n_distinct(doc_missing$doi)` papers. For these objects, no description or wiki was
assessed. This may be intentional and does not affect the license analysis.

writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session_info.txt")
